feat(game): local games can run a round clock (#457)

* feat(game): local games can run a round clock

A countdown starts from the minutes left on the venue clock, or a stopwatch
counts up. The clock shows in the match label at both ends of the board, the
top copy turned to face the far player. When time is called it walks the
end-of-round turns: five in Magic, three plus 15 minutes of overtime in
Pokémon, none in Yu-Gi-Oh!. The clock is stored as timestamps, so only taps
save, and only the label re-renders each second.

table is 0x28b304 itself (any id, not only 0x79), called only from the
network pump, which runs before each simulation step's world update. So
message 0x30's handler sets "in use" before the shell's update, and the
pod computer cannot see it a frame earlier: part 52's candidate for the
remaining tick is ruled out. Research only, no code change.

SNES arps carry the chord's 7th or 9th

Game-music arps on strings and harps nearly always include a colour tone;
a run on the bare triad sounds like a music box. In the SNES palette the
figure's octave-root step now becomes the chord's 7th or 9th, alternating
by bar, placed just above the triad so the shimmer sits on top. The tones

and phrygian a flat 9th rather than a wrong note; the lower steps keep the
triad. chip and genesis stay on triads, where the same notes clash on
square waves.

Warn before a stale handheld save can overwrite real progress

A handheld that has been offline keeps an old copy of each save. If a game
is launched on it before Syncthing catches up, the emulator writes that old
copy with a fresh timestamp, and Syncthing's newest-timestamp tiebreak then
makes it win everywhere, demoting the real progress to a conflict copy. The
tiebreak is not configurable, so the only prevention is knowing a device is
behind before it writes.

SaveSyncMonitor polls Syncthing once a minute for every device with a
